How Let’s Try Tripled Revenue To Cross ₹200 Cr In A Year

His early efforts focussed on aggregating and repurposing food waste at a local level, gradually evolving into a more structured operation. Dave and Kasturirangan crossed paths while working with a cloud communications startup, where close collaboration led to a shared understanding of supply chain inefficiencies.

As the duo worked closely with farmers, vendors and small businesses, they started building early supply loops, connecting waste generators with feed producers. Kasturirangan, who was initially involved as an investor, later recognised the scale of opportunity and came on board as a cofounder, helping formalise and scale the venture.

Over time, the company pivoted from broader waste categories such as plastic or e-waste to focus exclusively on food waste. This allowed Wastelink to build depth in sourcing, processing and standardising food waste streams, while also aligning more closely with the needs of feed manufacturers. In doing so, it began repositioning waste as a reliable alternative feed input.

“Solving for supply-demand mismatch was only one part of the problem. The bigger challenge lay in building trust across both sides of the value chain,” said Dave. He listed some of the key challenges Wastelink is solving for the ecosystem through its tech play.

For food businesses, the concern is not just disposal, but misuse. Once surplus exits their system, the risk of it entering informal, or even unauthorised, secondary markets becomes real. To address this, Wastelink has embedded traceability into its operations, enabling suppliers to track how their surplus moves through the chain and where it ultimately ends up.

Its reverse-logistics AI tool manages and records waste pickups from food producers. Materials are digitally tagged and tracked from collection through processing, maintaining visibility into the chain of custody. All of this is accessible through Wastelink’s dashboard, where suppliers can monitor the movement and status of their surplus in real time.

At the processing stage, batches are standardised using AI-driven nutrition formulation tools. This ensures consistent feed ingredients and allows the company to produce targeted outputs, such as a protein meal for weight gain, an energy meal for faster growth, or a sugar meal (a molasses alternative).

As a result, both food producers and feed manufacturers can access the auditable trail that tracks the journey from the original food source to the final feed ingredient supplied to manufacturers.

The biggest challenge for Wastelink lies in moving this highly perishable material quickly and efficiently. Wastelink does not own a fleet. Instead, it works with subcontracted transporters. The control sits firmly with its in-house intelligence layer.

Its in-house AI-powered reverse logistics system decides what to pick, when to pick and how to move it. The system factors in multiple variables, such as supplier readiness, traffic conditions, perishability of the material, vehicle capacity, and cost efficiency, to optimise routes and schedules. The idea is to lower logistics costs, increase fleet utilisation, reduce spoilage and ensure that waste reaches the facility within a viable window.

Once the material reaches the factory, the second layer of technology comes into play – standardisation. Food waste, by nature, is inconsistent, with no two batches being identical.

To address this, Wastelink has built a formulation engine that uses AI to analyse incoming material for nutritional value, moisture levels and variability. Based on this, it determines how different inputs can be blended to create a stable, standardised output — reducing reliance on manual formulation.

To ensure consistent quality, every batch undergoes multiple checkpoints: at the point of input, during processing and at the final output stage. Any material that fails to meet microbiological or safety standards is rejected. Even after this, feed manufacturers carry out their own validation before integration.

Scaling In An Unstructured Market

The ₹403.5 Cr animal feed market in India ranks among the largest globally, with projections for 15% growth by 2027. The organised sector has so far supplied only 50% of poultry feed and 10% of cattle and aqua feed in India.

As Wastelink scales, it steps up the focus on building a structured business in a largely unorganised category. The model sits at the intersection of surplus sourcing, scientific processing and feed integration, making operations complex.

Compliance spans multiple frameworks, especially as rules around food waste continue to evolve. Wastelink says it aligns its processes with existing animal feed standards, especially around quality and safety.

The company works with 25–30 suppliers, while steadily expanding its processing capacity. Wastelink aims for revenue of ₹35–40 Cr this financial year, though profitability remains a work-in-progress due to ongoing investments in capacity and quality systems.

The company has chosen to remain B2B-first, positioning ecoFeed as an ingredient within the existing supply chain, rather than building a consumer-facing brand and competing with existing players. Operationally, the model remains logistics- and labour-intensive, employing nearly 100 people directly and around 400 workers across factory operations.

Although food waste upcycling into feed inputs remains nascent in India, Wastelink faces indirect competition from players such as Billion Carbon and Carbon Masters, which convert food waste into manure and fertilisers. Unlike adjacent segments like plastic or e-waste recycling, this category lacks clear benchmarks and established leaders.

It will be interesting to see how Wastelink spins straw into gold by scaling efficiently while helping define processes and standards in a fragmented yet high-potential market.
